questions.question: What does an accepted response from the notification ingestion API guarantee?
options: Every provider has delivered the message to its destination.
The intent and publication record are durable under a stable notification ID.
Every recipient has passed the final send-time preference check.
All channel-specific templates have already been rendered.
questions.explanation: Acceptance ends at the durable intent and outbox boundary. Audience expansion, policy checks, rendering, provider calls, and final delivery happen asynchronously.

questions.question: Approximately how many notification intents per second does 100 million intents per day represent on average?
options: 116 intents/s
1,157 intents/s
11,574 intents/s
46,300 intents/s
questions.explanation: 100,000,000 divided by 86,400 seconds is about 1,157 intents per second. Peak planning is a separate multiplier.

questions.question: With 100 million daily intents, a 40x peak multiplier, and 1.4 eligible channels per intent, what peak provider-attempt rate should be modeled before retries?
options: About 1.6K attempts/s
About 46.3K attempts/s
About 64.8K attempts/s
About 140M attempts/s
questions.explanation: The average is about 1,157 intents/s; multiplying by 40 and then by 1.4 channels gives about 64,792 provider attempts/s.

questions.question: A user opts out of marketing email after the intent is queued but before the worker sends. What should the worker do?
options: Use the enqueue-time plan and send because the intent was already accepted.
Send once, then prevent only later retries.
Revalidate current policy, mark the delivery suppressed, and make no provider call.
Move the delivery to a dead-letter queue as a provider failure.
questions.explanation: The send-time policy decision is authoritative. Suppression is an intentional terminal outcome, not a failure that should be retried.

questions.question: A worker times out after a provider may have accepted its request. Which retry behavior best controls duplicate sends?
options: Create a new notification and a new provider key immediately.
Reuse the stable attempt key and reconcile provider status or retry idempotently.
Assume the send failed and switch channels without checking policy.
Mark the delivery permanently failed because its result is unknown.
questions.explanation: A timeout is ambiguous. Reusing the same attempt identity allows provider deduplication or status reconciliation without creating a second logical send.

questions.question: How should a provider adapter respond to an HTTP 429 with a Retry-After value?
options: Retry immediately on every worker until one request succeeds.
Pause all channels and all providers globally.
Ignore the value and use a fixed one-second retry interval.
Delay the affected provider partition, apply jitter and attempt limits, and keep other lanes draining.
questions.explanation: Provider quota feedback should contain pressure to the affected lane. Respecting Retry-After avoids a retry storm while preserving unrelated delivery capacity.

questions.question: Why is oldest eligible message age usually a better delivery alert than queue depth alone?
options: Age maps to the delivery SLO, while depth may include healthy future-scheduled work.
Age proves that every provider callback is authentic.
Depth cannot be measured in partitioned queues.
Age removes the need to monitor arrival and completion rates.
questions.explanation: A large queue may contain work scheduled for later, while a smaller queue of overdue critical messages is urgent. Age exposes the user-visible delay.

questions.question: A late provider callback reports accepted after the same attempt is already marked delivered. What should the status processor do?
options: Move the state backward to accepted because callbacks are authoritative.
Create a second channel delivery so both events are retained.
Apply the callback only if its state version is newer, regardless of transition validity.
Deduplicate the callback and reject the state regression while retaining an audit record.
questions.explanation: Provider callbacks may be duplicated or reordered. Delivery state must advance through valid monotonic transitions rather than following arrival order.
